doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Dream Band scale pay, writing the book and growing up with Tiny Kahn
summary: Gibbs recounts band pay of $11 at scale, why he wrote his book with Cary Ginell, and his boyhood friendship with Tiny Kahn and Tiny's influence.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Wow. And am I correct that when you were — the band was super popular yet the scale was $15 and you were lucky to make $11?

Well after the scale was 19 but I gave the band boy $8 and I made 11. And I was never happier in my whole life. You know what? I read — I didn’t start a band, it was a record date that started the band. I think — without having to explain the whole thing — I always tell people that I’m not trying to sell books because the book has been out since 2004, and I don’t get much money, if I ever did get much money from the book, I never wrote a book to make money. I wrote it because the publisher asked me and Cary Ginell, whose name I put on there, was a jazz historian. He called me and he said, “I’ll work with you on it” he says, you know. But when I say “work on it” I wrote every word in that book. Cary checked out every story, gave me some ideas. I was not going to write about my childhood, Monk. I was going to start out with the Charlie Parker, Benny Goodman, Steve Allen, Frank Sinatra. I was going to start out — he says, “No, you’ve got to write about your” — and after I wrote it, not realizing, I’ll even ask you, as you read my book, I had a crazy aunt I went to the movies with one time that stood up and screamed in the movies. Somewhere in your family you have a crazy uncle or a cousin, don’t you?

Everybody in the world has one. So, and you could relate to all, and all kids who play in the streets could relate to my stories, you know. So and I was lucky to have a great childhood. I grew up with Tiny Kahn, see Tiny Kahn is when I was from 6 years old until I went in the Army at 19 or 18, until I got with Woody Herman’s band really. We were together day and night. And if you can, people who know these names can imagine what we looked like at 15 years old, we looked like Peter Lorre and Sydney Greenstreet walking down the street. Tiny was about 6 foot 2 or something, but he wasn’t fat, he was big. And I was small, you know. And nobody wanted to hang out with Tiny. But I knew that he was musically, talent wise, I can’t use the word “genius” because he didn’t live that long. But if Johnny Mandel was alive or Al Cohn or Manny Albam, these great arrangers, they would tell you they learned arranging from what Tiny was doing. Mel Lewis will tell you he learned drums, the feel, from Tiny Kahn. Jeff Hamilton will tell you that Tiny Kahn, Mel Lewis, how it all started, and by the way you know why they played like that? Because I played that style of drums. Now Monk, you never ever heard me brag about my vibe playing. You never will you know. Half the time that I didn’t like what I played after I recorded. But when I was a drummer I was as good as any drummer playing today [phone ringing] — set this off because it’s probably nobody.
